bull.b: FDA approval converts the company’s core RAS/MAPK research into an approved commercial product for a high-need cancer indication. This creates a durable revenue platform and validates the company’s ability to advance targeted therapies through late-stage development and regulatory review.

Early revenue and patient uptake indicate meaningful initial demand for the approved therapy, while broad physician and payer access supports continued commercial expansion. Although launch cohorts may not persist, this adoption establishes a foundation for recurring treatment revenue as the eligible patient base develops.

A broad clinical portfolio reduces dependence on a single indication and preserves multiple paths to future growth. Progress across pancreatic, lung, colorectal, and earlier-stage RAS(ON) programs could extend the commercial opportunity and reinforce the company’s focused oncology capabilities over several years.

bear.b: The magnitude of negative cash flow and net losses means current operations consume substantial capital despite rising revenue. Continued burn increases dependence on financing and can constrain strategic flexibility, particularly while the company funds commercialization and several costly late-stage clinical programs.

Sustained and rising operating costs could keep profitability distant even after product launch. Higher research, development, commercial, and corporate spending raises the revenue scale required to achieve operating leverage, while also increasing the financial consequences if pipeline milestones or demand develop more slowly than expected.

Initial sales include temporary access-program transitions, early treatment cohorts, and channel stocking, so ongoing demand may be lower or slower to develop. Evolving payer policies and higher discounts could also reduce realized revenue per patient, making commercial forecasting and margin durability less certain.
